outputs.L1:
My old friend, I wonder how far north you have travelled? The road stretches west, beginning two doors up from the Dog's Bollocks and ending where the sun sets. So many sunsets that Facebook and Instagram together could not hold them all. So many yellow lines, so many white stripes, that scarcely a Valiant remains to defy them. Now the years catch up with us both.

As a boy, visits to Uncle Bruce and Aunty Lindy in their K'Rd council flat first revealed to me the grandeur of the great north, its dusty tail whipping all the way up to the skyline at Reinga. Yet why do I mistake your darkness for silence, my friend? You are a sleek black eel, pumping lifeblood all the way to Karekare, to Muriwai, to Bethells, to Piha—and our vehicles ride your surges back to K'Rd, back and forth, tirelessly, testing our shock absorbers and surfboards alike.

Keep bringing the waves, Great North Road. Keep saving the whales. Keep the toheroa gleaming, tucked safely away from spades in their sandy hideaways. Smile from your cars, and sound your horns—honk, honk, honk—along the Great North Road.

Continue delivering those waves, Great North Road. Continue protecting the whales! Continue sheltering the toheroa, safely hidden from digging tools in their sandy hideouts. Grin behind your steering wheels and sound your horns—honk, honk, honk—along the Great North Road.

**Great North Road**

I often find myself wondering how far north Great North Road truly goes—whether it simply fades into some other name at the city's edge, or whether it carries on, unbroken, all the way to places I've never seen. I trace it in my mind from near the Dog's Bollocks, that scruffy old pub standing sentinel at one end, and follow it westward, imagining it stretching on toward the kind of endless sunsets that swallow the sky in orange and violet before the world goes dark.

My connection to this road, and to the wildness it seems to promise, began long before I understood geography or distance. It started in childhood, on visits to Uncle Bruce and Aunty Lindy's council flat on K'Rd—that strip of the city thick with noise and neon and lives lived loudly. Sitting in their cramped kitchen, listening to grown-up talk drift over cups of tea, I'd catch mentions of the north—dusty, vast, untamed—stretching all the way up to Cape Reinga, where two oceans meet and the land runs out of places to go. Even as a kid, I sensed that greatness in the way people spoke of it, reverent and half-longing, as though the north held something the city could never quite offer.

To me, Great North Road became more than asphalt and painted lines—it became a companion, dark and silent, holding its secrets close. I picture it as a sleek black eel, slipping through the land, pumping life westward toward the beaches that give this city its wild heart: Karekare with its brooding cliffs, Muriwai and its gannets wheeling over black sand, Bethells with its dunes and its stillness, Piha with its roaring surf and the ever-watchful Lion Rock. The road carries something of the ocean in it, even far from the coast—an undertow, a pull, a promise of the wild.

Cars have changed since those days. The old Valiants that used to rumble down this stretch have long since vanished, replaced by sleeker, quieter machines gliding over crisp new road markings and freshly poured tarmac. The city has modernized around it, layer upon layer, but the road itself remains the same silent witness it always was. And still, the traffic surfs back and forth along its length—commuters, surfers, families, dreamers—flowing from the coast to K'Rd and back again, riding the road's dark current the way waves ride toward shore.

And so, I find myself offering something like a quiet prayer to this old road, half memory, half hope: keep bringing the waves, keep the whales safe as they pass offshore, let the toheroa continue burrowing undisturbed beneath the sand. Let the joy remain—the honking horns, the windows down, the grins exchanged between strangers heading the same way, chasing the same light. Let Great North Road keep doing what it has always done: carrying us toward something wild, something real, something worth remembering long after the drive is over.

# Great North Road

You've always been there, haven't you, old friend. Stretching your patient bitumen shoulders from the city's heart out toward the places where the land remembers what it was before we came and covered it with our houses and our haste.

I want to talk to you directly, Great North Road, because you deserve it. You were the road of my childhood, though I didn't know then to think of you as anything more than the way to Nana's house, the familiar landmarks ticking past the window—the dairy on the corner, the church with its peeling paint, the bend where Dad always slowed down for no reason anyone could explain.

I remember being small in the back seat, knees against vinyl, watching your service stations and your shop fronts blur into the rhythm of Sunday visits. You carried us to family—to aunties who pressed money into small hands, to uncles who talked too loud, to living rooms thick with the smell of Sunday roast and the murmur of grown-up conversation we weren't meant to understand.

But you were more than the road to family, weren't you. You were also the beginning of something larger—the first stretch of a longer journey north, toward Cape Reinga where the two oceans meet and argue at the tip of the land, toward the west coast beaches where the sand stretches black and endless and the surf comes in like it's been coming in since before there were roads at all.

I remember the excitement of those longer trips, when you were just the start, when your familiar shops gave way eventually to open country, to the smell of salt creeping into the car, to the first glimpse of dunes rising like sleeping giants. You led us toward toheroa dug from wet sand with cold hands, toward whales that sometimes beached themselves on those wild shores, mysterious and enormous, reminding us that the world held things larger than our small suburban lives.

You connected us to nature's treasures, Great North Road—not just the beaches and the shellfish and the whales, but to the vastness of the land itself, the sense that we were part of something that stretched beyond our windows, beyond our streets, beyond our understanding.

And you connected us to each other, too, across generations. My parents drove you as children, I suspect, watching the same corners, the same landmarks, though the shops have changed hands a dozen times since then and the cars have changed shape and the phones in our pockets now tell us where to turn instead of Dad's memory of the bend by the church.

Yet here you are still, patient and unchanging in your essential nature, even as everything around you transforms. The technology has changed—GPS instead of memorized turns, electric cars instead of the growl of Dad's old sedan—but you remain the same thread, connecting the same points, carrying new generations toward the same north, the same coast, the same whales and shellfish and endless sand.

I think that's what makes you significant, Great North Road, beyond your practical purpose of getting us from here to there. You're a kind of time made physical—a place where past and present overlap, where my childhood self and my adult self can somehow occupy the same stretch of road, where the journey to Nana's house and the journey to the cape become part of one continuous story.

You remind us that some things persist. That family visits and beach holidays and the particular quality of light on a New Zealand morning drive—these things connect us across years, across generations, even as the specific details fade and change. You are ordinary and extraordinary at once, Great North Road—just asphalt and painted lines, and also a thread that ties together everyone who has ever traveled you, going to see family, going to see the sea, going toward whatever waits at the end of the road, and the one after that, all the way to the top of the country where the land finally gives way to water and everything else.

# The Dog's Bollocks

The phrase "the dog's bollocks" is a colorful piece of British slang that means something is excellent, outstanding, or the best of its kind. Despite its crude-sounding origins, it's a well-established expression that has found its way into everyday conversation across the UK and other English-speaking countries.

## Origins and Etymology

The exact origin of this phrase is debated among linguists and word enthusiasts. Several theories exist:

1. **Typographical theory**: One popular explanation suggests the phrase originated from printing terminology, where a colon followed by a dash (:-) resembled a dog's testicles and was used to denote something of quality.

2. **Rhyming slang connection**: Some suggest it relates to other British expressions using animal anatomy to denote superlatives, similar to "the bee's knees" or "the cat's whiskers."

3. **Natural evolution**: Others believe it simply evolved organically as an exaggerated, humorous way to emphasize something being exceptional, playing on the absurdity and boldness of the phrase itself.

## Usage in Modern Context

Today, "the dog's bollocks" is used informally to praise:
- Products or services ("This new phone is the dog's bollocks")
- Performances or achievements
- Food or drink of exceptional quality
- Any situation where something exceeds expectations

## Cultural Significance

The phrase exemplifies British humor's tendency toward self-deprecating, cheeky, and irreverent expressions. It sits alongside other body-part idioms in English slang, showcasing how language often uses unexpected, sometimes crude imagery to convey enthusiasm and approval.

While the phrase might raise eyebrows in formal settings, it remains a beloved piece of colloquial English, demonstrating how slang can transform seemingly vulgar terms into affectionate, even charming expressions of praise.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem addressed to "Great North Road" in Auckland, blending personal memory with local geography and pop culture references.
counterfactuals.output:
# Ode to Great North Road

Great North Road, you eight-lane confession booth,
you strip of asphalt memory stretching from
Grey Lynn's villas to the Waterview cut,
where the tunnel swallows traffic like
a secret it promised to keep.

I have known you in the rain,
windscreen wipers keeping time with
whatever was playing on Mai FM,
some song about heartbreak that felt
too on the nose for a Tuesday.

You've watched me drive past
the Warehouse where I bought my first flat whites'
worth of secondhand vinyl,
past the New World where the trolleys
clatter like applause for nobody,
past St Lukes mall glowing at 9pm
like a spaceship that gave up on leaving.

Great North Road, you don't care about
my nostalgia — you've got Pt Chevalier
to worry about, and Western Springs
where the eels move slow as memory
in that green water, older than
any of our small griefs.

You are not glamorous.
You are not the harbour bridge at sunset,
not Instagram-famous like
K'Road's neon confessions.
You are the road my father drove
in his falcon ute, radio tuned to
the cricket, one arm out the window
like he owned the whole northwestern sky.

I have cried at your lights,
laughed at your lights,
sat so long at your lights
I've aged a season, watched
the pōhutukawa flare red
then fall like a match
struck and forgotten.

You go from Western Springs
to the city's teeth,
you carry the 18 bus like a rosary,
each stop a bead: Western Springs Rd,
Bond St, Newton — this
is how Auckland prays,
through gridlock,
through grace.

Great North Road, be honest —
did you know me before I knew myself?
Did you watch me become
someone who could leave this city
and someone who always,
always comes back?
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a nostalgic, stream-of-consciousness prose poem about growing up near K'Rd and driving out to west coast beaches like Piha and Muriwai.
counterfactuals.output:
# Karangahape Road, Then West

The neon still buzzed pink and green off wet pavement when I was small, held someone's hand—whose, I can't remember now, only the shape of being held—past the strip clubs waking up for evening and the church that never seemed to close its doors, both of them keeping their separate vigils on the same street like they'd made peace with each other decades before I was born. K'Rd smelled like frying oil and jasmine and something electrical, something that hummed under the footpath, and I thought that was just what the world smelled like, that every city breathed this particular exhale of vice and grace pressed together.

And then the cars, always the cars, someone's borrowed station wagon with the windows down because the AC never worked, and we'd peel off from the isthmus like the city was something to be shed, a good skin we didn't need for a few hours—out through the wilds of Titirangi where the road starts to forget it's a road and becomes something older, gravity pulling us down through bush so green it was almost black, nikau fronds clicking their applause as we passed, and the air changing, thickening with salt before you could even see water, that smell arriving like a memory before the actual memory does.

Piha unfolding black-sand and violent, Lion Rock standing there like it had opinions about all of us, the Tasman throwing itself against the shore not gently, never gently, this wasn't a postcard ocean, this was an ocean with teeth, and we loved it for that, we loved that it could kill you if you weren't careful, that respect was the entry fee. Someone always got pulled by the rip and someone always yelled and there was always that half-second of held breath before the swimmer stood up laughing, spitting saltwater, alive.

Muriwai further north or maybe it just felt that way, the gannets wheeling and screaming at the colony, their white bodies stitched into the cliff like the rock itself was trying to fly, and we'd eat hot chips gone soft with vinegar sitting on the bonnet of the car, watching the sun do its slow gold collapse into water that had no further coastline to hit, nothing between us and Australia but that huge blank assertion of ocean, and it made you feel small in the good way, the way that doesn't diminish you so much as remind you where you fit.

Driving back always in that particular dusk-blue, sand still between our toes, K'Rd waiting patient and unchanged, its lights coming on one by one like it had never once wondered where we'd gone.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a lyrical piece personifying a New Zealand road as an old friend, mixing humor, slang, and environmental concern for whales and toheroa.
counterfactuals.output:
# Ode to State Highway 1 (An Old Mate's Tale)

Oi, you old strip of chip-seal and dreams,
stretching from Cape Reinga down to nowhere-in-particular,
I've known you since I was a nipper in the back seat,
sicking up L&P on your corners,
and you never once complained, eh.

You're a good bastard, Highway.
Patient as a paddock full of sheep,
you've carried me past
Waitomo's glowworm dreamin',
through Taupo's steamy armpit,
and down that long, lonely stretch
where the radio gives up
and it's just you, me,
and a possum doing its best
impression of a speed bump.

But mate, I gotta ask —
you seen the whales lately?

Because I have. Or I haven't.
That's the bloody worry, isn't it.
The tohorā used to sing so loud
you could feel it in your foundations,
old friend, deep bass thrumming up through tar seal
like the whole coast was one big amp.
Now it's quieter.
Too quiet.
Like someone's turned the volume down
on the whole Pacific.

And the toheroa —
remember when Nana used to dig for them,
Ninety Mile Beach at dawn,
sand between her toes,
bucket clanking like a dinner bell?
Now you'd need a permit, a prayer,
and a fair bit of luck
to find enough for a feed.
They've gone quiet too.
Retreated like they know something
we're too flash with our ute exhaust
to notice.

Still, you keep rolling on, don't you,
you tough old taonga,
past the wind farms spinning like fidget toys for giants,
past the "SAVE THE WHALES" stickers
peeling off bumpers that never slow down,
past dairy runoff sneaking into streams
like a guilty secret.

I reckon you've got some sway, though, old road.
You're the spine of this whole skinny country,
carrying us from paddock to city to beach,
so how about you whisper it
through your tyre tracks and your painted lines:

Slow down.
Look sideways at the sea.
Give the whales their quiet back.
Let the toheroa breed in peace,
you flamin' legends of the shellfish world.

Because one day, old mate,
I want to bring my mokopuna down your length,
windows open, radio blaring some terrible Kiwi pop song,
and point out at that big blue paddock
and say —

look, there's a whale, breaching,
just like the old days,
still singing,
still ours to look after.

So here's to you, State Highway 1,
you weather-beaten, pothole-riddled legend,
carry us gently,
because the sea's listening too,
and it's about damn time
we gave it something good to hear.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental, emotionally layered ode to a specific Auckland street that moves between childhood memory, road trips, and reflections on time passing.
counterfactuals.output:
**Ode to New North Road**
*(for the six kilometres between Kingsland and the maunga you can't name right, still)*

—

You start as a bus number stencilled on the front of something
groaning, 2B, or was it the 22, the digits
rubbed soft by decades of thumbs pressing the yellow cord —
*this is my stop, this is my stop* —
and I am seven, and the doors sigh open onto
a strip of dairies and driveways and pōhutukawa
holding their red like a held breath before Christmas.

/

Odometer, 3.2 km: the corner where Dad
always slowed without saying why, some private ghost
of a car he used to own, or a girl, or a version
of himself still standing at that bus stop
in a school jersey two sizes ahead of him —
*I used to walk here*, he'd say, and the street
would keep driving, uninterested, forward.

/

New North Road, you are not one road.
You are the road my mother drove at speed
toward the hospital, hazards blinking apologies
at every red light, and you are the road
we crawled down after, three of us and a bassinet,
so slow the dairies seemed to lean in to look.

You are the road that becomes the motorway
becomes the causeway becomes the whole
green throat of the country opening north —
Ōrewa, Waipū, the family wagon packed
with a chilly bin and someone's carsickness bag,
*are we there yet* worn down to a joke worn down
to a silence worn down to sleep.

/

*[time passing, marked in shopfronts]*
— the video store is a nail bar
— the nail bar is a boba place
— the boba place has a queue at 4pm
   of teenagers who were, statistically,
   not alive when I was falling off my bike
   outside the still-there, always-there
   dairy with the broken freezer hum.

/

I want to tell you I remember every letterbox
but I don't. I remember the *feeling*
of letterboxes — small held breaths of red and silver,
the flag up meaning something was arriving,
some version of hope shaped like a bill or a birthday card.

I remember Maungawhau green and sudden
between the rooftops, the way a mountain can just
be *there*, mid-errand, unbothered by our smallness,
by the fact we were only nine, only late,
only trying to get to netball before the whistle.

/

Now I drive you at forty, in a car that isn't
my father's, isn't the one with the broken clock
stuck permanently at 8:15 — some morning
none of us can locate anymore —
and the street has widened, narrowed, widened,
the way memory does, the way a childhood does
when you try to drive back into it
and find the shortcut's been made one-way
against you.

/

Still: pōhutukawa in December,
unbothered by cul-de-sacs of feeling.
Still: the dairy, some dairy, any dairy,
selling penny lollies that cost more than a dollar now
but taste, I swear, exactly the same —
pineapple lump dissolving on a tongue
that used to be a child's and is now
just older, still mine, still asking
*are we there yet*
of a road that was never going anywhere
except forward, except through me,
except on.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a poetic monologue in a Kiwi voice reminiscing about family visits, beach trips, and cars, using vivid imagery and playful onomatopoeia like "honk honk honk."
counterfactuals.output:
# The Old Man's Yarn

Ah, mate, come sit a spell, let me tell ya bout the days when the Zephyr had that smell—
vinyl seats gone sticky in the summer heat, dust and salt and fish-and-chips all mixed up sweet.

We'd pile in like sardines, Nan up front with her floral scarf flapping,
Dad's elbow out the window, drumming on the door—*tap-tap-tap*—
and that horn of his, oh cripes, he loved that horn,
**honk honk honk** down every gravel road we'd born
past the paddocks, past the sheep going *baa* in reply,
like they were arguing with the sky.

The Bay was three hours if the old girl didn't overheat—
she'd wheeze and cough like Koro after a smoke,
steam hissing *pssshhht* from under the bonnet's cloak,
and we'd all pile out, stretch our legs on the tar seal,
watching Dad swear soft-like, checking the radiator's ordeal.

Then the beach—oh, the beach!—
sand so hot it'd have ya doing that hopping dance,
*ow, ow, ow* across the scorching stretch,
till the water hit your ankles, cold as Nana's judgment,
and the whole whānau'd be in, splashing, shrieking, laughing,
gulls wheeling overhead going *ark ark ark*,
stealing chips right off ya paper if you weren't quick in the dark
of that golden afternoon light, thick as honey, slow as time.

Uncle Bazza with his fishing rod, reckon he never caught a thing,
but he'd sit there yarning, letting the line just sing
in the wind, *whoosh*, out past the breakers,
while the kids built castles doomed to the tide's takers.

And the drive home, oh you'd fight to stay awake,
but the engine's hum, that steady old-car shake,
would rock ya under, salt-crusted and sun-drunk,
dreaming of golden sand and the old Zephyr's trunk
packed with togs and towels and a nannas of shells,
and somewhere in the dark, one last **honk honk honk**
as Dad'd wave to a mate on the roadside, just for the hell
of showing off that he'd made it, whole family intact,
home from the Bay, memories packed
tighter than the boot, richer than gold—
that's the story, mate. That's the story of old.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
